chunks: "Preemphasis is boosting the high-frequency content of the signal at the transmitter before it goes down a lossy channel.
The channel, whether it's a PCB trace, cable or backplane, acts like a low-pass filter: skin effect and dielectric loss attenuate high frequencies more than low.
If you send a clean square wave, the edges arrive slow and the energy of each bit smears into the next ones, which is inter-symbol interference, and the eye closes.
If I pre-boost the high frequencies by about the amount the channel will take away, the received spectrum comes out flat and the eye opens.
There are two ways of looking at it in the time domain. Preemphasis exaggerates the first bit after a transition.
De-emphasis lowers the amplitude of the bits that follow a transition when the data doesn't change. Same filter, just different reference level.
Implementation: usually a small FIR filter in the driver, two or three taps.
A 2-tap version is y[n] equals (1-a)x[n]-a x[n-1] : DC gain falls to 1-2a and the Nyquist gain stays 1, so that's a boost of 1 over (1-2a) at Nyquist, for example 6 decibels when a equals 0.
25 . You can also build it passively with a resistor in parallel with a capacitor in the driver's series path.
The cost is lower low-frequency amplitude or more power, more high-frequency EMI and crosstalk, and the coefficients have to be tuned per channel, which links do with training."
